templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. A customer asks whether an item can be ready today, but you have not checked the availability record. Your {lead} can help confirm the schedule.
templates.prompt: What is the best next step?

options.text: Tell the customer you will check with your {lead} before confirming a time.
options.why: Checking the schedule avoids making a promise the workplace may not be able to keep, while a clear update respects the customer's request.

options.text: Promise that it will be ready today so the customer can make plans.
options.why: You have not verified availability, so the promise could be inaccurate and create a larger problem.
options.misconception: A confident promise is good service even when the facts are unknown.

options.text: Tell the customer to call again later without checking the schedule.
options.why: This transfers the work to the customer and does not answer the request when you can seek the information.
options.misconception: Delaying a response is the same as resolving a question.

options.text: Guess based on how quickly similar requests were handled last week.
options.why: Past timing does not confirm today's availability or schedule.
options.misconception: A recent example is a reliable substitute for checking current information.

templates.principle: Give courteous service while verifying facts before making commitments on behalf of the workplace.

review.notes: The scenario says the schedule is unverified and identifies a source to check; it does not imply a specific availability outcome.

templates.timing: Verify the schedule before promising a completion time.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Client|a} comes to the counter upset, saying there is an error on {document|a}. They are speaking loudly, and other {client.plural} are waiting nearby.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Listen calmly without interrupting, apologize for the problem, and explain what you can do to fix it.
options.why: Letting the person finish shows respect, an apology acknowledges the problem, and a clear next step turns the conversation toward a solution.

options.text: Explain that the error was caused by another department, so they know it was not your fault.
options.why: Assigning blame does not solve the problem and can sound defensive. The person wants to know what happens next.
options.misconception: Explaining whose fault it was calms the person.

options.text: Ask the person to lower their voice before you agree to help with the problem at all.
options.why: Focusing on tone first can escalate frustration. Listening and offering a solution usually calms a situation faster.
options.misconception: Calm behavior has to come before good service.

options.text: Tell them the policy for errors and that there is nothing more you can do about it today.
options.why: Reciting a policy without offering anything makes the person feel unheard, and it ends the conversation without a solution.

templates.principle: Handle a complaint by listening, acknowledging the problem, and offering a clear next step instead of defending or deflecting.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You are in the middle of helping {client|a} when {coworker} from another team asks you for {document|a} that you are responsible for. {coworker} needs it by the end of the day, and you can finish with the {client} in about fifteen minutes.

options.text: Tell {coworker} you will have it done right after you finish with the {client}, and give a specific time.
options.why: Coworkers are internal customers. A clear time lets {coworker} plan, and finishing with the person in front of you keeps your service to them complete.

options.text: Stop helping the {client} and start on the {document} at once, since your coworker asked for it.
options.why: Walking away from someone midway through service is disruptive. The request is not due for hours, so it can wait a few minutes.
options.misconception: The newest request is the most urgent.

options.text: Keep helping the {client} and say nothing to {coworker}, since you will get to it eventually.
options.why: Not responding leaves {coworker} unsure whether the request was heard. A short answer with a time costs a few seconds and prevents follow-up.
options.misconception: A request that is not due yet does not need an answer.

options.text: Tell {coworker} to ask someone else, since you are busy serving the {client} right now.
options.why: Passing the request off ignores that {document|the} is your responsibility, and it forces your coworker to start over with someone else.
options.misconception: Customers outside the team always come first, so inside requests can be redirected.

templates.principle: Treat coworkers as customers too: acknowledge requests promptly and give a specific time when you cannot do them right away.
templates.timing: The coworker's request is not due immediately, so acknowledging with a time comes first.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Client|a} has been waiting for {document|a} and keeps glancing at the clock. You know the process needs about twenty more minutes to be done properly.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Let them know about how long it will take, and offer a place to wait or a way to be updated.
options.why: Telling a waiting person what to expect, without being asked, eases the frustration of not knowing and shows you noticed their need.

options.text: Keep working quietly, since stopping to talk would only slow down the process.
options.why: A short update takes seconds and helps the person plan their time. Silence leaves them guessing.
options.misconception: Working silently is the fastest service.

options.text: Tell them it will be done when it is done, since you cannot control how long it takes.
options.why: You do have an estimate, and sharing it respects their time. A blunt answer can sound dismissive.
options.misconception: If I cannot control it, I do not need to explain it.

options.text: Offer to speed things up by skipping a step in the usual process so they can leave sooner.
options.why: Skipping steps to save time risks errors, and the process takes twenty minutes to be done properly. Accuracy matters more than speed here.
options.misconception: Doing it faster is always better service.

templates.principle: Anticipate needs: tell waiting people what to expect and give them options, instead of leaving them guessing.

templates.scenario: A {client} wrote asking how to change an appointment at {workplace|the}. This is the reply from an employee.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is a problem.

segments.text: That is not my job, so you will have to figure it out yourself.
segments.why: Refusing to help or point the person to the right place leaves them stuck and reflects poorly on the whole workplace.

segments.text: I have attached the form for changing appointments.
segments.whyFine: Giving a useful resource answers the question directly.

segments.text: Please call us if you need anything else.

templates.principle: Good service means helping or pointing the person to who can; "not my job" leaves them stuck.

review.notes: Only one line refuses to help.

templates.scenario: {Client|a} comes to {workplace|the} with a complaint about a problem they had.
templates.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Listen to the whole complaint without interrupting
Acknowledge the problem and apologize for the trouble
Offer a solution, or find out who can provide one
Follow up to make sure the problem was resolved

precedence.why: You cannot acknowledge the problem until you have heard what it is.
People are more open to a solution after feeling heard.
You can only confirm resolution once a solution has been tried.

templates.principle: Handle complaints in order: listen, acknowledge, resolve, and follow up.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Client|a} asks for a refund but has no receipt. Your workplace's policy requires a receipt for refunds, allows exchanges without one, and lets your {lead} review special cases. The person is polite but disappointed.

options.text: Explain the policy kindly, offer an exchange, and offer to ask your {lead} to review their situation.
options.why: Following the policy while giving the person real options, including a review by your {lead}, treats them with respect and keeps your service within the rules.

options.text: Explain the policy kindly and tell them that the decision is final.
options.why: The explanation is courteous and accurate, but it leaves out the exchange and review options that the policy actually allows.

options.text: Give the refund anyway to avoid an awkward conversation, and hope that nobody notices.
options.why: Setting aside the policy on your own is unfair to others and can cause problems for you. A kind explanation with options is better.
options.misconception: A happy customer is worth bending any rule.

options.text: Tell them that policies are policies and that there is nothing more you can do about it.
options.why: Treating the policy as the end of the conversation ignores the options available and sounds dismissive.
options.misconception: Quoting the policy ends the conversation.

templates.principle: Explain limits kindly, offer every option the policy allows, and know who can review special cases.

review.notes: Policy stated in scenario; acceptable option omits allowed alternatives.
